draw_log.notes: Used: operation (trace a handover between people or services), ledger and a decade, which suggested a capacity finding copied from record to record over years. Rejected: a communication passport that travels with the person, because E149 (one-page baseline above the bed) already makes that argument.

Used: operation (an outcome patients value that the routine measure misses): the measure is that a letter reached the GP; the valued outcome is the person knowing what was found. Wall calendar and 'the first week' gave nothing. Rejected: 'patient experience surveys hear least from people with dementia', because I could not name a source for response rates by cognitive status (high evidence risk).

Recipe card, air traffic control, queuing and the paramedic viewpoint gave nothing usable; a paramedic non-conveyance idea was rejected as too close to C07-16 (write down why the person said no).

Door hinge, archives, borrowing, residue and 'a daughter, three months' gave nothing. Rejected: weekend decisions made with families by clinicians who do not know the person, because C07-11 covers out-of-hours visibility of wishes.

Bus pass, container shipping, signposting and thresholds gave nothing.

Hand mirror, cartography, rationing and a decade gave nothing.

Door hinge, orchestras, rewinding and three months gave nothing (three months suggested registration delays, but I had no verified current figure).

candidates.stimulus_use: Tracing a handover over a decade, with a ledger, suggested a capacity finding copied forward from record to record until it loses its decision and its date.
candidates.working_title: A capacity finding has a decision and a date
candidates.core_insight: A finding that someone lacks capacity applies to one decision at one time, so an old finding copied into a new admission, referral or care plan needs a fresh assessment before anyone relies on it.
candidates.angle: Capacity findings travel through handovers (hospital to care home, one admission to the next, one letter to another) and lose the two details that made them valid: which decision, and when. Over years a person can collect a record that says 'lacks capacity' as though it were a diagnosis.
candidates.position: A note saying 'lacks capacity' without the decision and the date should not be relied on; each significant decision needs its own assessment at the time it is made.
claims_needing_evidence: Under the Mental Capacity Act 2005, a person lacks capacity in relation to a matter if at the material time they are unable to make a decision for themselves in relation to that matter (statute, s2(1)).
The MCA Code of Practice describes capacity assessment as decision-specific and time-specific (official Code of Practice, chapter 4).

Scottish law under the Adults with Incapacity (Scotland) Act 2000 treats incapacity as relating to particular decisions or matters rather than to the person as a whole (statute and Scottish Government code of practice).
Capacity can fluctuate and can be regained, for example after acute illness (Code of Practice; clinical review).
evidence_leads: Mental Capacity Act 2005 s1(2), s2(1)
Department for Constitutional Affairs 2007, Mental Capacity Act 2005 Code of Practice, chapter 4 (paras 4.4 to 4.5) (unsure of paragraph numbers)
Adults with Incapacity (Scotland) Act 2000 s1(6) and the Scottish Government code of practice for medical practitioners (Part 5) (unsure of part number)
NICE NG108 (2018) Decision-making and mental capacity
Sessums LL, Zembrzuska H, Jackson JL 2011, JAMA 306:420-7, doi 10.1001/jama.2011.1023 (context: incapacity is common among inpatients and often temporary illness is involved)
candidates.opening_line_draft: A capacity assessment answers one question on one day.
candidates.visual_idea: Diagram, labelled 'Illustrative example': a timeline of four records (ward note, discharge letter, care home plan, next admission clerking). The first says 'Lacks capacity to decide on discharge destination, 3 March'; each later copy loses a piece until the last says only 'lacks capacity'. Final box: 'Which decision? Assessed when? Assess this decision, now.'
candidates.pause: Practitioners recognise the copied-forward phrase from letters and care plans they have read this week.
candidates.gain: A precise documentation habit and the legal basis for reassessing instead of inheriting a finding.
candidates.follow: The account gives exact, lawful capacity teaching that changes what people write in the notes.
candidates.earlier_overlap: none (the earlier collection has no capacity posts). Within C09, C09-15 makes the decision-specific point for families; this one is about records and time for practitioners.

candidates.stimulus_use: The operation 'find an outcome that patients value and the routine measure misses' pointed to clinic letters: the service counts a letter sent to the GP, while the person values knowing what was found and what happens next.
candidates.working_title: Ask for the clinic letter to be written to you
candidates.core_insight: You can ask for your hospital clinic letter to be written to you in plain language, with a copy to your GP, and national guidance from the Academy of Medical Royal Colleges recommends this.
candidates.angle: The letter is the only lasting record of a consultation most older people get, and it is usually written about them to someone else. A 2026 analysis of 4.6 million UK eye clinic letters found only a small fraction were addressed to patients, and most were harder to read than recommended.
candidates.position: Clinic letters should be written to the patient, in words they can use, and older people are entitled to ask for this.
claims_needing_evidence: The Academy of Medical Royal Colleges (2018) guidance 'Please, write to me' recommends that outpatient clinic letters be written directly to patients (official guidance).

In 4.6 million ophthalmology clinic letters written at Moorfields Eye Hospital from 2013 to 2025, about [N to verify] in 100 were addressed directly to patients and about [N to verify] in 100 were less readable than recommended (cohort analysis, Ong 2026).
In a urology quality improvement project, most patients who received a letter written to them found it easy to understand and said it improved their understanding of the visit (Lonergan 2019).
Patients who need a different format (large print, easy read) can ask for letters in that format (Accessible Information Standard, England; Equality Act 2010 reasonable adjustments).

Ong AY et al 2026, BMJ Health Care Inform 33(1), doi 10.1136/bmjhci-2026-102086 (about 2.25% addressed to patients; 95.3% less readable than recommended, per abstract)
Lonergan PE et al 2019, BMJ Open Qual 8:e000721, doi 10.1136/bmjoq-2019-000721

Right: 'Dear Mrs Grant, Today we talked about your dizziness. What we found... What happens next... Who to call...'. Footer question: 'Could you write the letter to me, please?'
candidates.pause: Many older people have never read the letter written about them, or found it hard to read when they did.
candidates.gain: A specific request, and the national guidance that supports it.
candidates.follow: Questions that change what people actually receive from services.
candidates.earlier_overlap: none

candidates.stimulus_use: The quality 'first impressions', with the operation comparing a stated aim with what happens, pointed to the gap between the law's ban on judging capacity from appearance and the first impressions that decide who gets a communication check.
candidates.working_title: First impressions in a capacity assessment
candidates.core_insight: How a person looks, sounds or behaves at first meeting tells you little about their capacity for a particular decision; the law in England and Wales says so, and research shows staff skip communication screening when a person seems fine.
candidates.angle: First impressions mislead in both directions: a fluent, sociable person may be unable to weigh a decision, and a deaf, slow or dishevelled person may be fully able. In a 2020 study, professionals chose not to screen communication when they judged it intact, and half of the unscreened patients with dementia or memory impairment turned out to have significant communication needs.
candidates.position: Capacity judgements should rest on the decision-specific test, with communication support offered to everyone, and never on how the person comes across.
claims_needing_evidence: Mental Capacity Act 2005 s2(3): lack of capacity may not be established merely by reference to a person's age or appearance, or a condition or aspect of behaviour that might lead others to make unjustified assumptions (statute).

In a mixed-methods case series, professionals chose not to use a communication screening tool when they perceived a patient's communication to be intact; four of eight patients with dementia or memory impairment who were not screened had significant communication needs (Jayes 2020).
People with dementia can retain social conversational skills that mask cognitive deficits, sometimes called a 'social facade' (observational studies).
Clinicians recognise incapacity in fewer than half of medical inpatients who lack it (systematic review, Sessums 2011).
evidence_leads: Mental Capacity Act 2005 s2(3)
Jayes M, Palmer R, Enderby P 2020, Int J Lang Commun Disord 56:90-101, doi 10.1111/1460-6984.12585
Sessums LL et al 2011, JAMA 306:420-7, doi 10.1001/jama.2011.1023 (clinicians recognised incapacity in 42% of affected patients)
Studies of the 'social facade' in Alzheimer's disease, e.g. Mograbi DC et al (unsure of year and journal)
candidates.opening_line_draft: The Mental Capacity Act says lack of capacity may not be decided from a person's age, appearance or behaviour alone.
candidates.visual_idea: Comparison card with two respectful drawn figures: one well dressed and chatting easily, one in a hospital gown leaning in to hear. Under each, the same label: 'First impression: tells you little'. Beneath both, the four questions the test asks: understand, retain, use and weigh, communicate. Source line: MCA 2005 s2(3); Jayes 2020.
candidates.pause: Most practitioners have heard 'she seems with it' used as a capacity judgement; the statute wording surprises people.
candidates.gain: A legal anchor and a reason to screen communication in every patient, including those who seem fine.
candidates.follow: Capacity teaching that uses the law and the research together.
candidates.earlier_overlap: E007 (a ten-minute conversation is not a dementia assessment) touches social skills masking deficits in diagnosis. This post is about capacity, runs in both directions, and rests on the statute and communication screening evidence.

candidates.stimulus_use: The operation 'look at what happens at night' pointed to conversations held when hearing aids are out and the room is dark.
candidates.working_title: At night, the hearing aids are out
candidates.core_insight: To speak to someone at night who has taken out their hearing aids, put light on your own face, get level and close, say their name first and use fewer words; for anything more than a quick check, offer the hearing aids and glasses first.
candidates.angle: Night-time talk (a medicine round, a check on pain, being woken at home) happens with hearing aids and glasses off and lights low, which removes the lip-reading and facial cues that people with hearing loss depend on. Raising the voice distorts speech; clear speech and a visible face help more.
candidates.position: For any conversation at night that needs an answer, offer the hearing aids and glasses first, or at least make your face visible and speak clearly.
claims_needing_evidence: Seeing the speaker's face improves understanding of speech, particularly in background noise (audiovisual speech perception research, Sumby and Pollack 1954).

Deliberately clear speech improved intelligibility for listeners with sensorineural hearing loss compared with conversational speech (Picheny 1985: about [N to verify] percentage points in five listeners).
Hearing aids are usually removed for sleep (audiology guidance).
Hearing loss is common in older age, affecting most people over 80 (population survey, e.g. Goman and Lin 2016).
evidence_leads: Sumby WH, Pollack I 1954, J Acoust Soc Am 26:212-5 (visual contribution to speech intelligibility in noise)
Picheny MA, Durlach NI, Braida LD 1985, J Speech Hear Res 28:96-103, doi 10.1044/jshr.2801.96
Goman AM, Lin FR 2016, Am J Public Health 106:1820-2, prevalence of hearing loss by severity in the US (unsure)
RNID communication tips for talking with people who have hearing loss (charity guidance)
candidates.opening_line_draft: At night the hearing aids are usually out and the lights are low, which is why a spoken question at the bedside often goes unheard.
candidates.visual_idea: Annotated scene: a dim bedroom or hospital bay at night. A carer or nurse sits at eye level beside the bed; a bedside lamp is angled so it lights the speaker's face, not the older person's eyes; the hearing aid case and glasses sit on the table within reach. Four short labels: 'Light on your face', 'Level and close', 'Name first', 'Few words, or offer the aids'.
candidates.pause: Night staff and spouses recognise the unanswered question in the dark.
candidates.gain: Four concrete actions that take seconds.
candidates.follow: Practical details that make everyday care work better.
candidates.earlier_overlap: E161 and E171 (hearing aids and amplifiers in hospital) argue for getting aids onto the ear. This post is about talking at night when the aids are out. Cross-category: C11-13 covers smoke alarms when aids are out.

candidates.stimulus_use: The operation 'compare what is recorded with what is experienced' pointed to a communication need recorded as a flag on the system while the letter that arrives ignores it.
candidates.working_title: Recorded as large print, sent in small print
candidates.core_insight: In England, NHS and social care services must identify, record, flag, share and meet a person's information and communication needs; the flag is where the duty starts, and you can ask for letters and information in a format you can use.
candidates.angle: What is recorded (large print, BSL interpreter, easy read, 'phone calls difficult, please text') can differ from what the person experiences (a standard-print appointment letter, a phone call they are unable to hear). Missed appointments and misunderstood instructions follow from the gap.
candidates.position: Recording a communication need without meeting it falls short of the Accessible Information Standard; older people and families can ask for the format they need and complain if it is ignored.
claims_needing_evidence: The Accessible Information Standard (NHS England, DCB1605, 2016) requires NHS and publicly funded adult social care providers in England to identify, record, flag, share and meet the information and communication needs of people with a disability, impairment or sensory loss (official document).
The standard has been reviewed and a revised version published (official document) (unsure of date).
Surveys or reviews have found that many people with sensory loss do not receive health information in formats they can use (Healthwatch or RNIB report) (unsure).
Outside England, the Equality Act 2010 duty to make reasonable adjustments applies to health services (statute).
evidence_leads: NHS England 2016, Accessible Information Standard DCB1605 specification and implementation guidance (revised 2017)
NHS England review of the Accessible Information Standard, 2022 to 2024 (unsure)
Healthwatch England report on accessible information (around 2022) (unsure of title)
RNIB reports on accessible health information for people with sight loss (unsure)
Equality Act 2010 s20 (reasonable adjustments)
candidates.opening_line_draft: A health record can say 'large print' and the next appointment letter can still arrive in small type.
candidates.visual_idea: Comparison: left, a simplified record screen with a flag 'Large print, 20 point. Phone calls difficult: use text.'; right, the envelope that arrives with small print and a missed-call icon. Beneath: the five steps of the standard as a row of labelled boxes (identify, record, flag, share, meet), with 'meet' marked as the step that was missed.
candidates.pause: People with sight or hearing loss, and their families, recognise the letter they could not read.
candidates.gain: The name of the standard and a specific request to make.
candidates.follow: Rights explained in practical terms.

candidates.stimulus_use: The same operation, with the care home manager viewpoint and 'the first week', pointed to moves recorded as ordinary discharges when the legal authority for moving a person who lacked capacity was missing.
candidates.working_title: Moved to a care home without lawful authority
candidates.core_insight: When an adult who lacks capacity to decide where to live moves from hospital to a care home, someone needs lawful authority for that move; a Mental Welfare Commission for Scotland review of moves in spring 2020 found some had none.
candidates.angle: The record says 'discharged to care home' or 'family agreed'. The Commission looked at what legal basis existed and found moves with no lawful authority and gaps in staff understanding of the law. For the person, it is a move they may not have chosen, with rights they may not have been told about.
candidates.position: A move to a care home for someone unable to decide needs a lawful basis and the person's involvement; a record that the family agreed is not the same thing.
claims_needing_evidence: The Mental Welfare Commission for Scotland 2021 report 'Authority to discharge' reviewed moves of adults who lacked capacity from hospital to care homes in Scotland between March and May 2020 (official document).
The review found [N to verify] moves that were unlawful and many records with inadequate information on the legal basis (official document).

In Scotland, a relative cannot lawfully agree to a care home move on behalf of an adult who lacks capacity unless they hold a relevant welfare power of attorney or guardianship (Adults with Incapacity (Scotland) Act 2000) (statute and guidance).
Legal standards for assessing capacity to decide where to live were not routinely applied on English hospital wards (ethnographic study, Emmett 2013).

Adults with Incapacity (Scotland) Act 2000; Social Work (Scotland) Act 1968 s13ZA and Scottish Government guidance on its use (unsure of guidance date)
Emmett C, Poole M, Bond J, Hughes JC 2013, Int J Law Psychiatry 36:73-82, doi 10.1016/j.ijlp.2012.11.009
candidates.opening_line_draft: In spring 2020, some people in Scotland were moved from hospital to care homes with no lawful authority for the move, a Mental Welfare Commission review found.
candidates.visual_idea: Diagram: a simple flow from a hospital bed to a care home door, with three questions at the door: 'Can the person decide this?', 'If not, what is the legal authority? candidates.gain: Three questions to answer before any move of a person who lacks capacity.
candidates.follow: Careful reading of official reports, without overstatement.

candidates.stimulus_use: The operation 'examine a neglected consequence' with the home care worker viewpoint pointed to what short visits remove: the time to offer choices and ask consent.
candidates.working_title: A short visit leaves little time for choice
candidates.core_insight: Offering choices and asking consent during personal care takes time, especially for people with dementia or hearing loss, so very short home care visits push care workers towards doing things to a person rather than with them.
candidates.angle: Visits are commissioned and counted in minutes and tasks. What gets squeezed is invisible in that count: the person's everyday decisions about when to get up, what to wear and whether to wash now. NICE advises against visits under 30 minutes except in narrow circumstances, and says people with cognitive impairment or communication difficulties may need more time.
candidates.position: Home care visits should be long enough for the worker to offer choices and wait for an answer; very short slots undermine the person's everyday decisions and put care workers in an unfair position.
claims_needing_evidence: NICE NG21 (2015) recommends that home care visits shorter than half an hour be made only when specific conditions are met, and that visit length take account of cognitive impairment, communication difficulties or sensory loss (official guideline).
Short visits of about 15 minutes remain in use in parts of UK home care (survey or official data) (unsure).
Strategies that help people with Alzheimer's disease understand, such as simple sentences and repetition, take extra time in conversation (observational study, Small 2003).
Home care workers report that time pressure limits person-centred care (qualitative study) (unsure).

UK Homecare Association or Unison survey on visit lengths (unsure)
Small JA, Gutman G, Makela S, Hillhouse B 2003, J Speech Lang Hear Res 46:353-67, doi 10.1044/1092-4388(2003/028)
Qualitative studies of home care for people with dementia, e.g. Leverton M et al 2021 (unsure)
candidates.opening_line_draft: 'Would you like to get up now, or in ten minutes?' is a question a 15-minute visit may not have time to wait for.
candidates.visual_idea: Diagram: a clock face showing a short visit divided into labelled segments (medicines, wash, breakfast, notes). Around the rim, the questions the person needs time to answer ('now or later?', 'which cardigan?', 'shall I help with that?') are shown pushed outside the circle.
candidates.pause: Care workers and families recognise the rush; it names the cost without blaming the worker.
candidates.gain: A clear argument, with the NICE recommendation, for giving visits enough time.
candidates.follow: Respect for care workers, with attention to the conditions that help or obstruct good care.
candidates.earlier_overlap: none

candidates.stimulus_use: The operation 'reveal what is omitted', with 'reversibility', pointed to the realistic options and the support attached to them, which are often missing from capacity assessments about going home.
candidates.working_title: Assess the decision against the options that exist
candidates.core_insight: When assessing someone's capacity to decide whether to go home, they must be given the realistic options, including the support that would be in place, because a person can only weigh what they have been told.
candidates.angle: Assessments sometimes ask 'Can you manage at home?' with no description of the care package, equipment or alternatives. In CC v KK (2012) the Court of Protection found an older woman with dementia had capacity to decide to return home, and stressed that the options must be put to the person. A 2024 study of recorded capacity assessments found options were not always presented.
candidates.position: A capacity assessment about where to live that does not present the realistic options, with the support attached to each, is an unfair test of the person's ability.
claims_needing_evidence: Mental Capacity Act 2005 s3(4): the information relevant to a decision includes the reasonably foreseeable consequences of deciding one way or another, or of failing to decide (statute).

In CC v KK and STCC [2012] EWHC 2136 (COP), Baker J held that KK had capacity to decide where to live and said the person should be presented with detailed options so their ability to weigh them can be fairly assessed (judgment) (check exact wording).
In video-recorded capacity assessments of patients with acquired brain injury, option-listing varied and options were not always presented (conversation analysis, Foulkes 2024).
Legal standards for assessing capacity to decide place of residence were not routinely applied on English hospital wards (ethnography, Emmett 2013).

candidates.stimulus_use: The operation 'reveal what is omitted' with the daughter viewpoint pointed to what goes missing when a relative comes to the appointment: the older person's own voice.
candidates.working_title: Going with a parent to an appointment, without taking over
candidates.core_insight: When you go with an older relative to an appointment, you help most by prompting them to speak and asking their opinion; in a US study, patients whose companions did this were more likely to take an active part in decisions.
candidates.angle: About four in ten routine medical visits in pooled studies were accompanied, and clinicians tend to turn to the companion. Specific companion behaviours (asking the patient questions, prompting them to talk, asking what they think) go with more patient involvement, while controlling or siding with the doctor goes with less.
candidates.position: A companion's job is to help the person speak for themselves; families can plan this before the appointment.
claims_needing_evidence: In 13 contributing studies, the weighted mean rate of accompaniment to routine adult medical visits was about 4 in 10; companions were mostly spouses or adult children (meta-analytic review, Wolff and Roter 2011).
When a companion was present, clinicians gave more biomedical information (Wolff and Roter 2011).

In videotaped geriatric primary care visits with 93 patients, those whose companions asked them questions, prompted them to talk and asked their opinion were more likely to be active in decision-making (cross-sectional; association, not proof of cause) (Clayman 2005).
Companions also showed autonomy-detracting behaviours such as controlling the patient or building alliances with the doctor (Clayman 2005).

Wolff JL, Roter DL 2011, Soc Sci Med 72:823-31, doi 10.1016/j.socscimed.2011.01.015
Laidsaar-Powell RC et al 2013, Patient Educ Couns, systematic review of triadic consultations (unsure of volume)
candidates.opening_line_draft: If you go with your mother to the doctor, one of the most useful things you can say is: 'What do you think, Mum?'
candidates.visual_idea: Three-panel comic strip labelled 'Illustrative example'. Panel 1: the doctor speaks to the daughter, the older woman looks on. Panel 2: the daughter moves her chair beside her mother and says 'Mum, tell her about the mornings.' Panel 3: the mother talks to the doctor while the daughter writes notes. candidates.pause: Older people recognise being talked over; relatives recognise doing it without meaning to.
candidates.gain: Specific things to do and say at the next appointment.
candidates.follow: Practical help for families that keeps the older person at the centre.
candidates.earlier_overlap: E160, E194 and E195 give relatives vocabulary for speaking up on a ward. This post is about helping the older person speak for themselves in a routine appointment.

candidates.stimulus_use: The last week of life and the night nurse viewpoint, with the operation comparing a stated aim with what happens, pointed to people talking about a dying person over the bed as if they were absent.
candidates.working_title: Keep talking to someone who is dying
candidates.core_insight: Some people who are dying and no longer respond may still hear; a small EEG study found brain responses to sound in unresponsive hospice patients, so saying who you are and explaining care before touching is worth continuing.
candidates.angle: The saying that hearing is the last sense to go is old; the direct evidence is small and shows the brain responding to sounds, which is not proof of understanding. That is still reason enough to speak to the person as someone present, and to avoid discussing them over the bed.
candidates.position: Speak to a dying person who no longer responds as though they may hear you. This is an ethical judgement supported, but not proven, by the evidence.
claims_needing_evidence: In an EEG study, most unresponsive, actively dying hospice patients showed automatic brain responses (mismatch negativity) to changes in tones, and some showed later responses linked in healthy people to conscious detection (Blundon 2020; number of unresponsive patients [N to verify]).
These responses show that the auditory system processes sound; they do not show that the person understands speech (paper's discussion).
End-of-life care guidance encourages staff and families to keep speaking to the dying person (NICE or palliative care organisation guidance) (unsure of wording).

candidates.stimulus_use: The quality 'permission' and the son viewpoint, with the operation comparing a stated aim with what happens, pointed to services asking the attorney for permission while the person could still decide.
candidates.working_title: A welfare power of attorney waits until you are unable to decide
candidates.core_insight: A health and welfare power of attorney (England and Wales) or welfare power of attorney (Scotland) can be used only for decisions you are unable to make yourself; while you can decide, the decision is yours and staff should ask you.
candidates.angle: Families and services sometimes treat the registered document as moving decisions to the attorney ('her son has power of attorney, ask him'). The document exists to protect the person when they are unable to decide; it gives the attorney no say over decisions the person can still make. Financial powers work differently, which is part of the confusion.
candidates.position: Services should ask the person first; holding a welfare power of attorney gives no authority over a decision the person can make.
claims_needing_evidence: Mental Capacity Act 2005 s11(7)(a): a lasting power of attorney for personal welfare authorises decisions only where the donor lacks capacity, or the attorney reasonably believes they do (statute).

Adults with Incapacity (Scotland) Act 2000: a welfare power of attorney is not exercisable unless the granter is incapable in relation to the decision, or the attorney reasonably believes so (statute, s16(5)) (check subsection).
A property and financial affairs lasting power of attorney in England and Wales can be used while the donor has capacity, with their permission (Office of the Public Guardian guidance).
In Scotland, a continuing (financial) power of attorney can be used from registration unless the document states otherwise (Office of the Public Guardian Scotland guidance).

candidates.stimulus_use: The occupational therapist viewpoint, with the operation 'reveal what is omitted', pointed to observed performance of real tasks, which is often missing from capacity assessments about living at home.
candidates.working_title: Ask them to show you as well as tell you
candidates.core_insight: Some people, often with impairment of planning and self-monitoring (executive function), can describe how they would manage at home yet are unable to do it; for decisions about living at home, watching a real task, often with an occupational therapist, shows whether the person can use what they know.
candidates.angle: Capacity interviews reward fluent answers, while the 'use or weigh' part of the test is where people with executive impairment struggle, and it is visible mainly in action. A failed task alone does not show incapacity: the next step is to show the person what was observed and see whether they can weigh it.
candidates.position: For decisions about living at home, capacity assessments should draw on observed function and put those observations to the person before any conclusion.
claims_needing_evidence: Mental Capacity Act 2005 s3(1)(c): a person is unable to decide if unable to use or weigh the relevant information as part of the process of making the decision (statute).
People with executive dysfunction may answer questions correctly in interview but fail to act on the same knowledge, sometimes called the frontal lobe paradox (neuropsychology literature).
Everyday decision-making ability in older people with cognitive impairment relates to executive function (validation study of a capacity tool such as ACED) (unsure).
Courts in England have considered 'executive capacity' when deciding capacity about care and residence (case law) (unsure of cases).

candidates.working_title: Agree what would reopen the decision
candidates.core_insight: When an older person with capacity chooses to live with a risk, a useful plan records what they understood, what would make the risk smaller and which specific changes would prompt everyone to talk again.
candidates.angle: Without agreed triggers, families and services either re-argue the choice at every visit or wait for a crisis. Naming the triggers in advance (a second fall, weight loss, a night spent on the floor) and who will notice them (for example the home care worker) respects the decision and keeps people involved.
candidates.position: Respecting a risky choice should include agreeing review triggers with the person, which avoids both repeated pressure and walking away.
claims_needing_evidence: Mental Capacity Act 2005 s1(4): a person is not to be treated as unable to make a decision merely because it is unwise (statute).
Department of Health 2007 guidance 'Independence, choice and risk' supports agreeing risk plans with the person and reviewing them (official document).
Adults with Incapacity (Scotland) Act 2000 principles and Scottish adult support guidance support involving the person in plans about risk (statute and guidance) (unsure of specific guidance).

candidates.stimulus_use: The operation 'change the scale' moved a pooled finding about unrecognised incapacity among inpatients down to the next consent form on a ward round.
candidates.working_title: Incapacity goes unnoticed when people agree
candidates.core_insight: Across inpatient studies, about a quarter of medical inpatients lacked capacity for treatment decisions and clinicians recognised it in fewer than half; people who agree to what is proposed are the least likely to be checked.
candidates.angle: Capacity tends to be questioned when a patient refuses. At the population scale, the missed cases are those who say yes without understanding, which means consent forms signed by people unable to give consent.
candidates.position: Consider capacity for every significant decision, including when the person agrees; agreement is not evidence of capacity.
claims_needing_evidence: In a systematic review, incapacity for treatment decisions was found in about [N to verify] in 100 medical inpatients, compared with about 3 in 100 healthy older controls, and clinicians recognised it in [N to verify] of affected patients (Sessums 2011).
In 302 acute medical inpatients in London, at least 40% were estimated to lack capacity, and clinical teams identified 12 of the 50 interviewed patients who lacked it (Raymont 2004).
Refusal of treatment commonly triggers a capacity assessment, while agreement rarely does (review or guidance) (unsure of source).

MCA Code of Practice chapter 4 (when to assess)

candidates.gain: A reason to check capacity when patients agree, not only when they refuse.
candidates.follow: Reading the evidence posts turn a statistic into a change in practice.

candidates.stimulus_use: The operation 'find the first question worth asking' pointed to the question a family should ask when told a relative 'lacks capacity'.
candidates.working_title: Ask: capacity to make which decision?
candidates.core_insight: If you are told your relative 'lacks capacity', ask which decision this refers to; capacity is judged decision by decision, and the person may still be able to make many other choices, which they should be helped to make.
candidates.angle: Families often hear the phrase as a verdict on the whole person. Asking 'for which decision?' reopens everything else the person can still decide: what to eat and wear, who visits, whether to see the GP, how to spend money day to day.
candidates.position: A finding of incapacity for one decision should not remove a person from other decisions they are able to make.
claims_needing_evidence: Under the Mental Capacity Act 2005, capacity is assessed in relation to a particular decision at a particular time (statute s2(1); Code of Practice chapter 4).

Under the Adults with Incapacity (Scotland) Act 2000, anyone acting must take account of the adult's past and present wishes and encourage the adult to use the skills they have (statute s1(4) and s1(5)).
A person may lack capacity for a complex decision and still have capacity for simpler ones (Code of Practice examples).

Adults with Incapacity (Scotland) Act 2000 s1(4), s1(5)

candidates.gain: A single question that keeps the person involved in their own life.
candidates.follow: The Ask this series gives questions people can use straight away.

candidates.stimulus_use: The older person viewpoint, with 'returning' and 'handovers', pointed to an outcome people value that nothing measures: getting decisions handed back after recovering from a serious illness.
candidates.working_title: When you recover, the decisions come back to you
candidates.core_insight: If decisions were made for you while you were too unwell to make them, they become yours again once you recover, and you can ask what was decided, why, and whether it still stands.
candidates.angle: During a serious illness, a team may decide things in a person's best interests after talking to family: a medicine stopped, a resuscitation decision, a referral for a care home assessment. When the person recovers, nobody routinely hands these back, and nothing records whether it happened.
candidates.position: Once someone is able to decide again, decisions made on their behalf should be explained to them and reviewed with them.
claims_needing_evidence: Mental Capacity Act 2005 s4(3): anyone deciding in a person's best interests must consider whether the person is likely to regain capacity and, if so, when (statute).
The MCA Code of Practice says that when a person regains capacity they should make the decision themselves (official Code, chapter 5) (unsure of paragraph).
GMC guidance says that when a patient regains capacity they should be told what was done while they lacked it and why (official guidance) (unsure of wording).
Resuscitation decisions should be discussed with the patient when they are able to take part (Resuscitation Council UK, BMA and RCN joint guidance).

GMC 2020, Decision making and consent (unsure of paragraph)

Adults with Incapacity (Scotland) Act 2000 s47 (certificates of incapacity, duration and review)

candidates.working_title: Remembering the decision later is a different question
candidates.core_insight: In England and Wales a person needs to retain the relevant information only long enough to make the decision, so forgetting the conversation afterwards does not by itself mean they lacked capacity; notes and reminders can help them hold on to it.
candidates.angle: Families and staff often say 'she won't remember we talked about it, so she is unable to decide'. The law sets the bar at the decision itself, and memory aids are part of supporting it. Scotland's statute uses different wording ('retaining the memory of decisions'), so the post names its jurisdiction.
candidates.position: Poor memory alone should not exclude a person from a decision; record the decision in a way the person can look back at.
claims_needing_evidence: Mental Capacity Act 2005 s3(3): being able to retain the relevant information for a short period only does not prevent a person from being regarded as able to make the decision (statute).
The MCA Code of Practice suggests aids such as notebooks, photographs or recordings to help a person retain information (official Code, chapter 4) (unsure of paragraph).
The Adults with Incapacity (Scotland) Act 2000 s1(6) defines incapable as including 'retaining the memory of decisions', so the wording and interpretation differ in Scotland (statute).

candidates.gain: An accurate reading of the law and a practical memory aid.

candidates.working_title: Elderspeak and refusal of care
candidates.core_insight: Talking to older people with dementia in a sing-song, 'sweetheart', 'shall we' style is linked with more resistance to care, and a three-session staff training course reduced both in a cluster randomised trial in nursing homes.
candidates.angle: Elderspeak is usually meant kindly and is almost universal in recorded care. The evidence treats it as a care-quality problem: in video studies resistance was more likely after elderspeak than after normal adult talk, a hospital study found the same link, and a short training programme changed staff talk and residents' responses.
candidates.position: Elderspeak should be treated as a care-quality problem with a tested remedy, not as a matter of manners.
claims_needing_evidence: In 80 videotaped care episodes with 20 nursing home residents with dementia, the probability of resistiveness to care was about 55 in 100 after elderspeak and about 26 in 100 after normal talk (Williams 2009).

In a cluster randomised trial in 13 nursing homes (CHAT), staff elderspeak fell by about [N to verify] percentage points after training and resident resistiveness by about [N to verify] percentage points, with effects persisting at 3 months (Williams 2017).

In 88 recorded hospital care encounters with people with dementia, nearly all included some elderspeak, and less elderspeak was associated with lower odds of rejection of care (observational, Shaw 2022).
Elderspeak features include diminutives ('honey', 'dear'), collective pronouns ('we'), tag questions and exaggerated pitch (definitions used in these studies).

candidates.working_title: What helps people with Alzheimer's follow what you say
candidates.core_insight: For people with Alzheimer's disease, short simple sentences and repeating or rephrasing helped understanding in small studies, while speaking more slowly on its own did not.
candidates.angle: 'Speak slowly' is the advice carers hear most. An experiment found repetition, in the same or different words, improved comprehension and slow speech did not; a study of couples recorded at home found simple sentences worked and slow speech did not. Research in older adults generally found high pitch and a slow rate made people report more communication problems.
candidates.position: explanatory, no position
claims_needing_evidence: In an experiment with 15 people with mild to moderate Alzheimer's disease, comprehension improved when a sentence was repeated verbatim or paraphrased but not when it was spoken slowly (Small, Kemper and Lyons 1997).
In 18 couples recorded at home during daily activities, simple sentences were an effective strategy and slow speech was not (Small 2003).

In older adults without dementia, reducing embedded clauses helped communication, while short sentences, slow rate and high pitch did not and led to more reported communication problems (Kemper and Harden 1999).
These studies are small and short-term (limitation to state).

candidates.working_title: Hearing loss is missing from communication research
candidates.core_insight: A systematic review found that fewer than a quarter of studies of doctors' communication with older patients mentioned hearing loss at all, although hearing loss affects most people over 80.
candidates.angle: Communication with older people is studied and taught with hearing left out of the count: some studies excluded people with hearing loss, and very few measured it. The practical corollary is to check hearing at the start of any conversation that matters for a decision.
candidates.position: Studies, audits and teaching about communication with older people should measure hearing, and clinicians should check hearing before judging understanding.
claims_needing_evidence: Of 67 studies of physician communication with older patients published since 2000, 16 mentioned hearing loss; 4 used it as an exclusion criterion, 2 measured it without further analysis, 3 examined its association with communication and 1 included an intervention (Cohen 2017).
Most adults aged 80 and over have bilateral hearing loss (US population survey; primary source needed rather than the review's introduction).
Only a minority of older adults with hearing loss use hearing aids (population survey).

candidates.working_title: Aphasia and capacity assessment
candidates.core_insight: People with aphasia after a stroke have difficulty with language, which is different from difficulty with judgement, and many can take part in decisions when information is given in a form they can use; speech and language therapists can help, but are often not asked.
candidates.angle: Capacity assessments are conducted almost entirely through talk, so people with aphasia risk being judged unable when the difficulty is the channel. Screening tools and speech and language therapy input exist; an international survey of therapists found other professionals often do not seek their involvement.
candidates.position: When a person has aphasia, involve a speech and language therapist or use structured communication support before concluding they lack capacity.
claims_needing_evidence: Aphasia affects the understanding and use of language and does not in itself mean loss of decision-making ability (clinical and legal literature).
Aphasia affects about [N to verify] in 100 people after stroke (systematic review).
In an international survey of 195 speech and language therapists, barriers to supporting decision-making included other disciplines not seeking their involvement (Jayes 2026).
Health professionals without specialist training had difficulty identifying communication difficulties before capacity assessments (Jayes 2020).

Mental Capacity Act s1(3) requires all practicable steps to help a person decide; the Adults with Incapacity (Scotland) Act s1(6) excludes communication difficulties that can be made good by human or mechanical aid (statutes).

candidates.working_title: Talking Mats: a low-tech way to include people with dementia
candidates.core_insight: Talking Mats, a picture-based framework developed in Scotland, helped people with dementia and their family carers feel more involved and more satisfied in discussions about daily living than their usual way of talking.
candidates.angle: Supported decision-making can be practical and cheap. In an evaluation with 18 couples at home, both partners rated their involvement higher when using the mats. The study was small and did not test long-term outcomes, which the post should say.
candidates.position: explanatory, no position
claims_needing_evidence: In 18 couples (a person with dementia and a family carer) in Scotland and northern England, both felt more involved and more satisfied with discussions of personal care, getting around, housework and activities when using Talking Mats than with their usual communication (within-couple comparison, Murphy and Oliver 2013).
Talking Mats was developed at the University of Stirling and is run by the Talking Mats Centre (organisation information).
The evaluation was small, short-term and not randomised (limitation).

Murphy J, Gray CM, Cox S 2007, Joseph Rowntree Foundation report on Talking Mats and dementia (unsure)

candidates.pause: Carers who struggle to discuss care with a partner see a concrete method.
candidates.gain: A specific tool, with an honest statement of how strong the evidence is.

candidates.working_title: Teach-back: what the newest review found
candidates.core_insight: A 2026 meta-analysis of 18 randomised trials found no clear effect of teach-back (asking patients to explain back what they have been told) on their knowledge, with low to very low certainty evidence of better confidence and short-term adherence.
candidates.angle: Teach-back is widely taught as a proven way to improve understanding. The trials do not show that clearly. Its strongest justification may be as a check on the clinician's explanation, finding out what was missed, rather than as a test the patient passes.
candidates.position: Keep using teach-back to check your own explanation, but avoid claiming it has been shown to improve what patients know.
claims_needing_evidence: In 18 RCTs with 1985 participants, there was no clear pattern of effect of teach-back on knowledge (very low certainty); teach-back increased self-efficacy (5 RCTs, very low certainty) and self-reported short-term adherence (7 RCTs, low certainty), with wide confidence intervals and substantial heterogeneity (Vick 2026).
Patients forget a large share of medical information soon after a consultation, and older age is associated with poorer recall (review, Kessels 2003).
Teach-back is recommended in NHS health literacy guidance (official guidance) (unsure of document).
evidence_leads: Vick JB et al 2026, J Gen Intern Med, doi 10.1007/s11606-026-10678-y
NHS England or Health Education England health literacy resources recommending teach-back (unsure)
Schillinger D et al 2003, Arch Intern Med 163:83-90, physician communication and diabetes outcomes (observational) (unsure of pages)
candidates.opening_line_draft: Teach-back is often taught as a proven way to improve understanding. A 2026 review of 18 trials found no clear effect on what patients knew.
candidates.visual_idea: Comparison chart in three rows: 'Knowledge: no clear pattern (very low certainty)', 'Confidence: increased (very low certainty)', 'Adherence, short term: increased (low certainty)'. Certainty shown by word labels and a pattern, not colour alone. Footer: 'Use it to test your explanation.' Credit: Vick et al, J Gen Intern Med 2026.
candidates.pause: It questions a technique most clinicians were taught as settled.
candidates.gain: A calibrated view of a common technique and a better reason to use it.
candidates.follow: Reading the evidence posts separate what is shown from what is assumed.

candidates.working_title: When you are asked what she would want
candidates.core_insight: If a doctor asks what your relative would want, you are being asked about their wishes and values; unless you hold legal authority, such as a welfare power of attorney, the treatment decision rests with the clinical team, not with you.
candidates.angle: Relatives often feel they are being asked to decide, for example about resuscitation, and a systematic review found at least a third of people making decisions for others had lasting distress. Knowing what the person wanted was the most commonly reported thing that eased it. Clarity about whose decision it is helps both the person and the family.
candidates.position: Clinicians should say clearly whose decision it is; relatives can answer about the person rather than about their own preference.
claims_needing_evidence: Mental Capacity Act 2005 s4(6) and s4(7): a best-interests decision must consider the person's past and present wishes, feelings, beliefs and values, and consult carers and family about them (statute).

Unless a relative holds a health and welfare lasting power of attorney or is a court-appointed deputy (England and Wales), or holds welfare powers as attorney or guardian (Scotland), the clinician makes the treatment decision, after consultation (statutes; Scotland s47 AWI).

In 40 studies of 2854 people who made treatment decisions for incapacitated adults, at least one third experienced negative emotional effects, often lasting months; knowing which treatment matched the patient's preferences was often cited as reducing them (Wendler and Rid 2011; mostly US studies).
GMC guidance advises that relatives should not be given the impression that they are being asked to make the decision (official guidance) (unsure of wording and document).
evidence_leads: Mental Capacity Act 2005 s4(6), s4(7)
Adults with Incapacity (Scotland) Act 2000 s1(4), s47
GMC 2010, Treatment and care towards the end of life; GMC 2020, Decision making and consent (unsure which contains the wording)
candidates.opening_line_draft: 'What would your mother want?' is a question about her. Unless you hold legal authority, the decision itself stays with the medical team.
candidates.visual_idea: Question card: 'What would she want?' in large type. Below, two labelled boxes. 'What you can tell them': what she said before, what she valued, how she lived, what she feared. 'Whose decision it is': the medical team, unless you are her welfare attorney or guardian. Footnote on jurisdiction.
candidates.pause: Families in hard conversations often carry a weight they were never meant to carry alone.
candidates.gain: Clarity about their role, and what to say.
candidates.follow: Explanations that help families at the hardest moments.
candidates.earlier_overlap: E116 (tell the surgical team who the person was last week) is about giving baseline information. This post is about the family's role in best-interests decisions. Cross-category: C07-11 covers making wishes visible to out-of-hours clinicians.

candidates.working_title: Relatives predict treatment wishes correctly about two times in three
candidates.core_insight: In a systematic review, relatives and chosen proxies predicted patients' treatment preferences correctly about two times in three, and having discussed the preferences beforehand did not improve accuracy.
candidates.angle: Planning for incapacity usually rests on someone close knowing what the person wants. The evidence suggests they will often be wrong about specific choices, even after a conversation. The implication is to record the person's own views while they can give them, and to ask relatives about values and past statements rather than to guess a choice.
candidates.position: Seek and record the person's own views while they are able to give them; treat relatives' predictions as useful but fallible.
claims_needing_evidence: In 16 studies with 2595 patient and surrogate pairs responding to hypothetical scenarios, surrogates predicted patients' treatment preferences with 68% accuracy (Shalowitz 2006).
Neither being chosen by the patient nor prior discussion of preferences improved surrogates' accuracy (Shalowitz 2006).
The studies used hypothetical end-of-life scenarios, mostly in the US (limitation).
evidence_leads: Shalowitz DI, Garrett-Mayer E, Wendler D 2006, Arch Intern Med 166:493-7, doi 10.1001/archinte.166.5.493
Wendler D, Rid A 2011, Ann Intern Med 154:336-46 (related: effect on surrogates)
candidates.opening_line_draft: In 16 studies, relatives asked to predict a patient's treatment choices got about two in three right.
candidates.visual_idea: Icon array of three pairs of figures: two pairs with matching answer cards, one pair with different cards. Beside it: 'Talking about wishes beforehand did not improve accuracy in these studies.' Below: 'Write down your own views, and why.' Credit: Shalowitz et al, Arch Intern Med 2006.
candidates.pause: Most people assume their family knows what they would want.
candidates.gain: A reason to record wishes in the person's own words, and a better question for relatives.
candidates.follow: Reading the evidence posts that change how readers plan.
candidates.earlier_overlap: none. Within C09, C09-24 covers the family's legal role; this post covers the accuracy evidence.

candidates.working_title: An MMSE score is not a capacity assessment
candidates.core_insight: Cognitive screening scores help only at the extremes: in a systematic review, MMSE scores of 20 to 24 did not change the likelihood that a patient lacked capacity, so a decision-specific assessment is always needed.
candidates.angle: A common shortcut writes 'MMSE 22, lacks capacity' or 'MMSE 28, has capacity'. Pooled data show that scores below 20 make incapacity more likely and scores above 24 make it less likely, while the middle band gives no information; an earlier study in Alzheimer's disease found scores of 21 to 25 did not separate capable from incapable patients.
candidates.position: A cognitive test score can prompt or inform a capacity assessment but should never replace it.
claims_needing_evidence: In a systematic review, MMSE scores below 20 increased the likelihood of incapacity (likelihood ratio about 6), scores of 20 to 24 had no effect (about 0.9), and scores above 24 lowered it (about 0.14) (Sessums 2011).
In 37 patients with mild to moderate Alzheimer's disease, MMSE scores of 21 to 25 did not discriminate capacity status well (Kim and Caine 2002).
The Aid to Capacity Evaluation (ACE) had useful test characteristics and is freely available (Sessums 2011).
evidence_leads: Sessums LL, Zembrzuska H, Jackson JL 2011, JAMA 306:420-7, doi 10.1001/jama.2011.1023
Kim SY, Caine ED 2002, Psychiatr Serv 53:1322-4, doi 10.1176/appi.ps.53.10.1322
Etchells E et al 1999, J Gen Intern Med, validation of the Aid to Capacity Evaluation (unsure)
candidates.opening_line_draft: An MMSE score between 20 and 24 tells you almost nothing about whether a patient can make a treatment decision.
candidates.visual_idea: Diagram: an MMSE scale bar from 0 to 30 divided into three labelled zones: 'Below 20: incapacity more likely', '20 to 24: no information', 'Above 24: incapacity less likely'. Over the whole bar: 'Then assess the decision.' Zones distinguished by label and pattern. Credit: Sessums et al, JAMA 2011.
candidates.pause: Practitioners see MMSE scores quoted as capacity findings in letters.
candidates.gain: A precise reading of what a screening score can and cannot add.
candidates.follow: Teaching round posts qualify common shortcuts with data.
candidates.earlier_overlap: E015 (an MMSE of 26 does not close the case when the family describes decline) concerns dementia diagnosis. This post concerns capacity and the uninformative middle band.

candidates.working_title: Deaf patients who use BSL need an interpreter, not a notepad
candidates.core_insight: For many Deaf people who use British Sign Language, English is a second language, so written notes are an unreliable substitute for a qualified BSL interpreter in health conversations.
candidates.angle: Pen and paper is often the first thing offered. BSL is a language with its own grammar, recognised in UK and Scottish law, and written English with medical terms may be hard for many Deaf signers. Older Deaf people face this at the moments when decisions are hardest.
candidates.position: Book a registered BSL interpreter for health conversations with Deaf BSL users; written notes or relatives are inadequate for significant decisions.
claims_needing_evidence: BSL is recognised as a language in law by the British Sign Language (Scotland) Act 2015 and the British Sign Language Act 2022 (statutes).
Many Deaf BSL users have English as a second language, and written English may not be accessible to them (published commentary and research, e.g. Alexander 2012).
Deaf people in the UK report communication barriers in health care and have poorer health outcomes on some measures (survey or cohort study, e.g. SignHealth 2014; Emond 2015) (unsure).
The Accessible Information Standard in England covers BSL interpretation as a communication need (official document).
evidence_leads: Alexander A, Ladd P, Powell S 2012, Lancet 379:979-81, doi 10.1016/S0140-6736(11)61670-X
British Sign Language (Scotland) Act 2015; British Sign Language Act 2022
SignHealth 2014, 'Sick of it: how the health service is failing Deaf people' (unsure of title)
Emond A et al 2015, BMJ Open, health of the signing Deaf community in the UK compared with the general population (unsure)
NHS England Accessible Information Standard DCB1605
candidates.opening_line_draft: Pen and paper is often the first thing offered to a Deaf patient who uses British Sign Language. For many, written English is a second language.
candidates.visual_idea: Comparison: left, a clinician writing a note full of medical terms for a Deaf older man; right, a BSL interpreter standing next to the clinician, facing the patient, so the patient can see both. Footer: 'Ask for a registered BSL interpreter.' Accurate positioning of the interpreter.

candidates.gain: A clear request to make, with the legal recognition behind it.
candidates.follow: Who gets left out posts on people poorly served by routine practice.
candidates.earlier_overlap: E159 and E021 cover spoken-language interpreters. This post is about Deaf BSL users.

candidates.working_title: Covert medicines: a decision with rules
candidates.core_insight: Giving medicines hidden in food or drink to someone who lacks capacity to refuse them can be justified, but only after a capacity assessment, a best-interests decision involving the prescriber, a pharmacist and family, a written plan for each medicine and a set review date.
candidates.angle: The benefit (treating pain, seizures or Parkinson's disease in someone who refuses tablets they need) has to be weighed against deception, loss of trust and the practical risks of crushing or mixing. The process protects the person, and it also removes medicines that are not worth the deception.
candidates.position: Covert medication is a last resort that needs a documented lawful process and regular review; it should never be used for convenience, and each medicine on the list should be justified.
claims_needing_evidence: NICE SC1 (2014) states that covert administration should be used only for people who lack capacity, after a best-interests meeting involving care staff, the prescriber, a pharmacist and family, with the decision recorded and reviewed (official guideline).

The Mental Welfare Commission for Scotland good practice guide on covert medication requires lawful authority under the Adults with Incapacity (Scotland) Act, pharmacist advice and review (official document) (unsure of latest edition).
Research in UK care homes has found covert medication practices that were inappropriate or not lawful (published studies) (Morris 2018 describes such research).
Crushing or mixing some medicines changes how they work or makes them unsafe (pharmacy guidance).
evidence_leads: NICE SC1 (2014) Managing medicines in care homes, recommendations on covert administration (section 1.15) (unsure of section number)
Mental Welfare Commission for Scotland, 'Covert medication: good practice guide' (2017, with later updates) (unsure of edition)
Care Quality Commission guidance on covert administration of medicines (unsure)
Morris JE et al 2018, Geriatrics (Basel) 3:78, doi 10.3390/geriatrics3040078
candidates.opening_line_draft: Hiding a tablet in someone's yoghurt is sometimes the right decision. It should never be one person's decision at a medicines round.
candidates.visual_idea: Checklist card with six items: 'Capacity assessed for this medicine', 'Best-interests meeting: prescriber, pharmacist, family, staff', 'Each medicine justified, and unnecessary ones stopped', 'Pharmacist advice on how to give it', 'Written plan', 'Review date'.

candidates.gain: A clear lawful process and permission to stop medicines that are not worth hiding.
candidates.follow: Weighing it up posts treat hard trade-offs with respect.

candidates.working_title: Two kinds of advance document
candidates.core_insight: In England and Wales, an advance statement of wishes guides decisions but is not binding, while a valid and applicable advance decision to refuse treatment is legally binding, and refusing life-sustaining treatment needs particular formalities; Scotland's law differs.
candidates.angle: People often believe everything they write about future care is binding, or that none of it is. The distinction tells them what to write, how to sign it and who needs a copy, and why reviewing an old document when health changes is worthwhile.
candidates.position: explanatory, no position
claims_needing_evidence: Mental Capacity Act 2005 ss24 to 26: an advance decision to refuse specified treatment is binding if it is valid and applicable (statute).
s25(5) and (6): an advance decision refusing life-sustaining treatment must be in writing, signed and witnessed, and include a statement that it applies even if life is at risk (statute).
Written statements of wishes must be considered in a best-interests decision (s4(6)(a)) but do not compel treatment (statute).
An advance decision may become invalid or inapplicable if the person later acts inconsistently with it or circumstances were not anticipated (s25(2) to (4)) (statute).

In Scotland, advance directives are not set out in the Adults with Incapacity Act but must be taken into account as the adult's past wishes; their binding status rests on common law (statute and guidance) (unsure).
evidence_leads: Mental Capacity Act 2005 s4(6)(a), ss24 to 26; MCA Code of Practice chapter 9
NICE NG108 (2018) Decision-making and mental capacity (advance care planning section)
Adults with Incapacity (Scotland) Act 2000 s1(4); Scottish Government guidance on anticipatory care planning (unsure)
Compassion in Dying guides to advance decisions (charity guidance) (unsure)
candidates.opening_line_draft: What you write about your future care can be one of two things: wishes that guide your doctors, or a refusal they must follow.
candidates.visual_idea: Comparison card with two columns. 'Advance statement': what you want and what is important to you; guides decisions; any format. candidates.pause: Many people have written something and are unsure what it does.
candidates.gain: A clear distinction and the formalities that make a refusal valid.
candidates.follow: Plain explanations of rights people can use.

candidates.working_title: Before assessing capacity, remove the obstacles
candidates.core_insight: The law requires all practicable steps to help someone decide before concluding they are unable to; a short routine (hearing aid in, glasses on, pain treated, right time of day, interpreter, quiet room, key points written, a trusted person present, enough time) covers most of them, and recording which were used shows it was done.
candidates.angle: Supported decision-making sounds abstract; in practice it is a list of ordinary things done before the conversation. Doing them changes the result for some people, and writing them down turns a legal principle into a checkable record.
candidates.position: A capacity assessment done without these supports is incomplete; the record should state which supports were given.
claims_needing_evidence: Mental Capacity Act 2005 s1(3): a person is not to be treated as unable to make a decision unless all practicable steps to help them have been taken without success (statute).
The MCA Code of Practice chapter 3 lists ways to help a person decide, including choosing the best time and place, appropriate communication and involving people the person trusts (official Code).
The Adults with Incapacity (Scotland) Act s1(6) excludes lack of communication that can be made good by human or mechanical aid (statute).
Hearing and vision impairment lower scores on cognitive tests, so uncorrected sensory loss can make a person appear less able (observational study, e.g. Dupuis 2015) (unsure).
evidence_leads: Mental Capacity Act 2005 s1(3); MCA Code of Practice chapter 3
NICE NG108 (2018), section on supporting decision-making (unsure of section number)
Adults with Incapacity (Scotland) Act 2000 s1(6)
Dupuis K et al 2015, Aging Neuropsychol Cogn 22:413-37, effects of hearing and vision impairment on the MoCA (unsure)
candidates.opening_line_draft: The Mental Capacity Act asks one question before any finding of incapacity: have you taken every practicable step to help the person decide?
candidates.visual_idea: Checklist card with nine tick boxes: hearing aid in and working; glasses on; pain treated; best time of day for this person; interpreter if needed; quiet room; key points written in large print; someone they trust present, if they want; time to think, or a second conversation. candidates.gain: A way to meet a legal duty and to show it was met.
candidates.follow: Care that works posts make good practice copyable.

candidates.working_title: A capacitous refusal is where the work starts
candidates.core_insight: When an older person with capacity refuses help at home, the refusal should be respected, and the work continues: exploring the reasons, offering different help, checking whether they can put their decisions into practice, and staying in contact; reviews of serious harm from self-neglect have repeatedly found cases closed too early.
candidates.angle: The presumption of capacity protects people from paternalism. A House of Lords committee found it was also sometimes used to justify non-intervention. Analyses of Safeguarding Adults Reviews on self-neglect describe refusals accepted as 'lifestyle choice' without anyone asking why.
candidates.position: Respecting a capacitous refusal includes continued contact and repeated, different offers; closing the case on the first refusal can amount to abandonment.
claims_needing_evidence: The House of Lords Select Committee on the Mental Capacity Act 2005 (2014) reported that the presumption of capacity was widely misunderstood and sometimes used to support non-intervention or poor care (official report).

Thematic analyses of Safeguarding Adults Reviews on self-neglect in England found recurring shortcomings, including limited exploration of capacity (particularly the ability to carry out decisions) and acceptance of 'lifestyle choice' (published analyses) (unsure of exact findings).
Care Act 2014 statutory guidance includes self-neglect as a category of abuse and neglect (official document).

candidates.working_title: Running an interpreted consultation for a big decision
candidates.core_insight: For a significant conversation with someone who has limited English, book a professional interpreter, brief them first, allow extra time, look at the patient and speak to them as 'you', and give information in short sections; professional interpreters are associated with better communication and care than ad hoc ones.
candidates.angle: Earlier posts argued for using interpreters. The practical gap is how: many clinicians address the interpreter, speak in long paragraphs and allow no extra time, which defeats the purpose in a capacity assessment or a treatment decision.
candidates.position: Professional interpreters should be used for capacity assessments and major treatment decisions, and the consultation should be planned around them.
claims_needing_evidence: In a systematic review of 28 studies, use of professional interpreters was associated with better communication (fewer errors, better comprehension), clinical outcomes and satisfaction than use of ad hoc interpreters (Karliner 2007).
Errors of potential clinical consequence were more common with ad hoc interpreters than with professional interpreters (Flores 2012) (unsure).
NHS England guidance advises against using family members or friends as interpreters except in emergencies (official guidance, 2018).
Interpreting guidance recommends pre-briefing, speaking in the first and second person and short segments (professional guidance) (unsure of source).
evidence_leads: Karliner LS, Jacobs EA, Chen AH, Mutha S 2007, Health Serv Res 42:727-54, doi 10.1111/j.1475-6773.2006.00629.x
Flores G et al 2012, Ann Emerg Med 60:545-53, errors of medical interpretation (unsure)
NHS England 2018, 'Guidance for commissioners: Interpreting and Translation Services in Primary Care'
NHS Scotland interpreting, communication support and translation national policy (unsure of date)
